spots.name: Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels
spots.label: Basílica de los Ángele

text.geographic_location: The basilica stands in the city of Cartago, in Costa Rica.
text.description:
The Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels is the Roman Catholic basilica of Cartago, dedicated to the Virgen de los Ángeles, a small figure of the Virgin Mary carrying the infant Jesus. The story goes that a peasant girl found the figure in Cartago. The basilica was built in 1639 and was partly destroyed by an earthquake. It has since been restored, and the current building dates from 1939. The result is a mix of colonial architecture and 19th-century Byzantine style, which gives you plenty of detail to photograph: towers, domes, decorated walls and doorways.

It photographs well because the building is large and richly detailed. Start with a wide shot to show as much of the building as you can, then move in for details such as the carved stonework, the towers and the roofline. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. If people are walking through the scene, wait a moment for a gap, or include them to show the size of the building. Check the official site before you go in case there are any rules about photography or visiting.
text.directions_text: From there, the middle of the basilica outline on the map is about 21 m to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The basilica is a place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a large building like this, and thin cloud also helps by avoiding harsh shadows. Visiting earlier in the day is likely to mean fewer people in your shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. If you want to include a lot of the surroundings, try panorama mode, and hold the phone steady while you sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Hold the phone upright and level. Leave a little space above the roofline. For a second shot, step in closer and use the telephoto to fill the frame with one tower or doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit as much of the building in as you can. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as towers, windows and carved decoration.

spots.name: Ruinas de Santiago Apóstol
spots.label: Ruinas de Cartago

text.description:
The Ruinas de Santiago Apóstol are the ruins of a building named after Saint James the Apostle, in Cartago. Ruins like this suit a phone camera because weathered stonework gives you strong shapes and textures, and the contrast between old stone and the greenery or sky around it makes a photo feel layered without any special effort.

The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north of the subject. From there the ruins are straight ahead of you, and you can see the structure as a whole. Start with a wide shot to show the setting, then move in for details such as the stone, any openings and any plants you can see on the walls. If you spot a doorway or arch, it may frame a second shot, with the main ruin behind it.

Keep an eye on other visitors in your frame. Waiting a few seconds usually gives you a clean shot, or you can include a person to show the scale of the walls. Wipe your lens before you start, as a smudge shows up badly against bright sky. Rules for entering the grounds can change, so check locally before you go.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, and no public transport stops are listed for it either, so head for the ruins in Cartago. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: Check locally for access rules before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on pale stone. Check the weather on the day, because cloud and rain change the mood.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Face south and the ruins are ahead of you. If you want a closer view, walk a few steps towards them, but this spot gives the clearest overall picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ruins to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stone stays visible. Portrait mode works well for a photo of a person standing in front of the ruins.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the main wall or other strong feature on one of the lines, leaving some sky above. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a second shot, if there is an opening or archway, use it to frame the ruins behind it. Take one wide shot and one close-up of the stone texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the ruins. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole structure in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details in the stonework without walking closer.

spots.name: Our Lady of Carmel Cathedral, Cartago
spots.label: Catedral de Cartago

text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the city of Cartago, in the canton of the same name in Costa Rica.
text.description: Our Lady of Carmel Cathedral, also called Cartago Cathedral, is the seat of the Catholic diocese of Cartago in Costa Rica. The diocese was created in May 2005 by Pope Benedict XVI. The building began as a parish church, built between 1954 and 1960, and it is counted among the two most important churches in the town, alongside the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels. Be careful not to confuse it with a church of the same name in Cartago, Colombia. For photographs, the map's stand-here point is in the Parque Central, the open square in front of the historic centre. From there you get a wide view of the plaza with its fountain and a large national flag, with the ruined Santiago Apóstol church behind. This is a good, easy scene for a phone. Please note that the cathedral itself is not confirmed to be in frame from this square, and the cathedral is a separate stop to the north-east. Treat the plaza as a scene-setting shot of Cartago, and check the framing on site if you want the cathedral in the picture. Keep your phone level with the gridlines on, and include a little foreground, such as the fountain, to give the image depth.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Parque Central in central Cartago. Head north-east and check the route on your phone's map as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The Parque Central is an open public square; for the cathedral, which is a place of worship, check the official site or the diocese before you go, and dress modestly.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the plaza. Check the sky on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parque Central. A wide view across the central plaza with its fountain and a large national flag, with the ruined Santiago Apóstol church as the backdrop; the cathedral itself is not confirmed in frame. From here the photo shows a wide view across the central plaza, with the fountain and the large national flag, and the ruined Santiago Apóstol church as the backdrop. The cathedral is not confirmed to be visible from this square, so check on site before counting on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the flag or the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky does not turn white. Try a Live Photo to catch the flag moving in the wind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the flag or fountain on one third line, with the ruins filling the background. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. If you move on to the cathedral, take a step back from the front and use the default lens (1x), then 2x for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the plaza, and switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the fountain, flag and ruined church all in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the ruins or the flag from a distance.
